summaries.example: Imagine a class of toys. You might say, “Every red toy is on the shelf,” or “Some red toy is on the shelf.” These statements talk about the toys themselves. First-order logic helps us write rules about objects and their relationships, such as “every child has a friend.”
summaries.summary: First-order logic is a way to describe objects and the relationships among them. Today it is often taught as a central system of logic, but its history was a long, winding process. George Boole used algebra to represent some kinds of reasoning. Charles Peirce later developed ways to represent relationships and statements about every object or at least one object. Gottlob Frege built a different logical system while trying to explain the foundations of arithmetic. Other logicians extended, organized, or criticized these ideas. Russell and Whitehead studied systems with several logical levels. Löwenheim and Skolem found important facts about what kinds of models first-order statements can have. Hilbert and Bernays made a major advance by treating logic as a formal system that could itself be studied. Gödel then proved a completeness result for first-order logic and helped reveal how it differs from stronger systems. The entry’s main lesson is that first-order logic became “natural” only after the fact. Its rise depended on both technical results and changing views about the foundations of mathematics.
key_ideas: First-order logic did not appear all at once or come from one person.
Boole connected logic with algebra; Peirce added relations and clear symbols for “every” and “some.”
Frege developed a different system that used functions and several levels of logical ideas.
Later thinkers, including Russell, Löwenheim, Skolem, Hilbert, Bernays, and Gödel, helped develop modern logic.
First-order logic became especially important after mathematicians studied its rules and models.
Its special status was not inevitable. Mathematical discoveries and philosophical goals both shaped its history.
summaries.why_it_matters: First-order logic gives mathematicians a careful language for describing objects, rules, and relationships. It also teaches a broader lesson about discovery: ideas that later seem obvious may have required many people, different approaches, and new questions before their importance became clear.

important_terms.definition: A formal way to make statements about objects, their qualities, and their relationships. Its quantifiers range over objects, not over properties or collections of properties.
A word or symbol that says how many things a statement concerns, such as “every” or “some.”
A system of symbols and rules used to decide whether reasoning follows correctly.
A collection of objects being discussed, such as all the books in a library or all the numbers in a problem.

questions_to_think_about: Why might “every” and “some” need special symbols in logic?
How is talking about objects different from talking about properties?
Why might people prefer a system that is easier to check, even if another system can say more?
Does a useful tool have to be the only correct tool?

summaries.example: Consider the difference between these claims: “Every student has a mentor” and “There is one mentor who has every student.” In symbols, the order of the quantifiers changes. The first allows different mentors for different students; the second requires a single mentor. The history of first-order logic includes learning how such structures can be represented and then studying what follows from the formal system.
summaries.summary: The entry argues that first-order logic was not simply discovered as a finished object. Its components developed through several partially independent lines of work. Boole represented aspects of reasoning algebraically. De Morgan and Peirce expanded attention to relations, and Peirce introduced notation for universal and existential quantification while distinguishing first-intentional from second-intentional logic. Frege independently combined relations and quantification in a formal system aimed at grounding arithmetic in logic. Schröder organized much of the Boolean and Peircean tradition, while Peano introduced influential notation without clearly separating logical orders. Russell and Whitehead developed type theory in response to paradoxes, but regarded the full hierarchy as part of logic. Löwenheim and Skolem proved results about the size of models of what we now recognize as first-order formulas. The decisive conceptual change came with Hilbert and Bernays: logic was presented as formal calculi whose syntax, semantics, and metatheoretical properties could be studied explicitly. Gödel’s completeness theorem and later results showed that first-order logic has distinctive properties, including completeness, compactness, and the Löwenheim-Skolem property. Nevertheless, higher-order systems remained attractive, especially when categoricity or greater expressive power was desired. First-order logic became standard through an interaction of technical achievements with philosophical concerns about paradoxes, foundations, constructivity, and the status of set theory.
key_ideas: The emergence of first-order logic involved separate traditions: Boolean algebra, the logic of relations, Fregean foundations, type theory, and Hilbert-style formal systems.
Peirce explicitly distinguished first-order from second-order logic in 1885, but that distinction did not immediately guide mathematical research.
Frege and Russell developed hierarchies of logical levels, yet their projects treated higher-order resources as part of logic rather than isolating first-order logic as privileged.
Löwenheim and Skolem obtained results that, in retrospect, concern first-order formulas, even though they did not initially frame their work as the study of a distinct first-order system.
Hilbert’s introduction of object-language, metalanguage, and explicit questions about consistency, completeness, and decidability made modern metamathematical study possible.
Gödel’s results exposed important differences between first-order and higher-order systems, but technical results alone did not force a single choice of logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history clarifies why first-order logic is central without treating that status as timeless or unavoidable. It also separates three questions: who first identified the system, when its differences from higher-order logic became mathematically clear, and why it came to be treated as privileged. More generally, the story shows that mathematical concepts are shaped by formal techniques and by assumptions about what mathematics should accomplish.

important_terms.definition: A formal logical system whose quantifiers range over individuals in a domain, while predicates and relations are not themselves among the quantified objects.
A logical expression such as universal “every” or existential “some,” used to indicate the range of a variable.
A logical system in which quantifiers may range over predicates, properties, or relations, not only over individual objects.
The study of formal systems by examining their symbols, proofs, interpretations, models, and properties such as consistency or completeness.
The result that every statement valid in all models of first-order logic can also be derived in an appropriate formal proof system, and conversely.
The fact that if a first-order set of sentences has a model, then it has a model with at most countably many objects in the relevant theorem.
A formal description of a domain together with an interpretation that makes its sentences true.
The view that there may be several useful logical systems rather than one uniquely correct logic for every purpose.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the order of universal and existential quantifiers matter?
Does a logic’s completeness compensate for its inability to characterize one unique model?
Why might quantifying over all objects seem clearer than quantifying over all properties of those objects?
Can practical usefulness justify calling one logical system “standard”?
What would a history centered on logical pluralism look like?

summaries.example: Suppose a coach says, “Every player has a teammate,” and another says, “There is one player who is a teammate of everyone.” These sentences are not equivalent. The first can involve many teammates; the second requires one person connected to all. First-order logic helps show this difference by carefully arranging words such as “every” and “some.”
summaries.summary: First-order logic is now a basic part of mathematical logic, but the entry explains that it did not emerge through one sudden invention. In the nineteenth century, George Boole represented classes and propositions with algebraic symbols. Augustus De Morgan and Charles Peirce developed ways to reason about relations, and Peirce later introduced clear notation for statements involving every object or at least one object. Independently, Gottlob Frege created a formal system connected to his attempt to build arithmetic from logic. Frege’s system included several levels of logical quantification, while Peirce more clearly separated first-order and higher-order ideas. Ernst Schröder organized much of the earlier algebraic work, and Giuseppe Peano introduced symbols that influenced later notation. Russell and Whitehead developed type theory after Russell’s paradox, but they viewed the whole hierarchy of types as part of logic rather than treating first-order logic as a separate favorite system. Löwenheim and Skolem proved important results about the models of formulas that we now call first-order. Hilbert and Bernays then introduced a clearer formal framework: a logical system could be written down, interpreted, and studied from the outside. Gödel’s completeness theorem and related results revealed that first-order logic has important properties, including compactness and the Löwenheim-Skolem property. Even so, higher-order logic can express more and can sometimes give stronger forms of uniqueness. First-order logic became standard because technical results combined with concerns about paradoxes, mathematical foundations, and the acceptability of quantifying over properties.
key_ideas: The development of first-order logic was gradual and involved several traditions that were not always connected.
Boole began with an algebra of classes and propositions, while Peirce expanded logic to relations and quantifiers.
Frege independently created a powerful formal language while trying to explain arithmetic through logic.
Russell and Whitehead used types to organize different levels of logical objects and to respond to paradoxes.
Hilbert and Bernays made logic into a formal object that could be tested with metamathematical questions.
Gödel’s work showed why first-order logic is technically distinctive, but philosophers and mathematicians still had reasons to consider higher-order logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history explains why modern logic uses first-order logic so often without claiming that it is the only possible logic. It also shows how new notation, proof methods, philosophical goals, and debates about the foundations of mathematics can work together to change what a field considers central.

important_terms.definition: A formal system for talking about individual things and their properties or relationships, using quantifiers such as “every” and “some.”
A word or symbol that tells us whether we mean all objects or at least one object.
A statement about how objects are connected, such as “is next to” or “is older than.”
A statement or rule that is true in a particular interpretation of the symbols.
The study of a logical system itself, including what can be proved, what is true in its models, and whether its rules work reliably.
A property of a formal proof system in which every statement true in all suitable models can be proved in the system.
A result saying, roughly, that certain satisfiable first-order descriptions have a model that is finite or countable in size, depending on the version of the theorem.

questions_to_think_about: Why would a logic need ways to express both relationships and quantities such as “all” and “some”?
What is gained by separating a formal language from the language used to talk about it?
Why might a system that cannot describe one unique model still be useful?
Should a logical system be chosen because it is strongest, easiest to study, or best suited to a purpose?
How can philosophical beliefs about mathematics influence technical research?
